Good morning, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Welcome back to the Plenary Meeting of the 2025 Annual Session of the UN Women Executive Board. I am Suela Janina, the Permanent Representative of Albania and Vice President of the Executive Board. Then the Executive Board will receive a presentation on the related management response and perspective. I am pleased to welcome today the following UN colleagues to the podium. Kirsy Madi, Deputy Executive Director for Resource Management, Sustainability and Partnership. Deputy Executive Director for Normative Support, UN System Coordination and Programme Results. Director, Policy, Programme and Intergovernmental Division. Director, Independent Evaluation, Audit and Investigation Services. Without any further ado, Ms. Sutter, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, members of the Executive Board, dear colleagues. Good morning. I have the pleasure of presenting the highlights from the Annual Report on the UN Women Evaluation Function. Evaluation supports the delivery of results by demonstrating accountability, providing evidence for decision-making, and contributing lessons for learning. In 2024, the Independent Evaluation Service advanced these objectives by completing corporate evaluations in the areas of women's political participation and social norms, a synthesis of UN system-wide evaluations related to SDG 5, and a formative assessment of the Gender Equality Accelerators. In addition, last year, 3 corporate evaluations were in progress on ending violence against women, sustainable finance, and support to women in peace processes. Moreover, a synthesis of UN Women's performance against the Strategic Plan was progressed to provide insight into the new Strategic Plan. At the decentralized level, 50 evaluations were conducted or in progress. The Independent Evaluation Service led or managed 18 strategic evaluations at the regional and country level, of which 6 country portfolio evaluations were completed, of UN Women's work in Niger, Burundi, Rwanda, Mali, Timor-Leste, and Syria program presence. In 2024, corporate evaluation performance indicators remained good. Financial resources spent on evaluation across UN Women represented 1.6% of program expenditure, falling short of the 2% minimum target. There is a need to ensure sustained investment and protection of evaluation resources. Evaluation quality remained high, with all completed evaluations rated either as very good or good. Human resources across UN Women for evaluation and evaluation implementation rates saw increases in 2024. Engagement in joint evaluations increased, accounting for 35% of all evaluations conducted across UN Women. In terms of evaluation coverage, all but 3 country offices had at least one evaluation during their strategic note cycle, and 2 of these offices have already initiated evaluation processes in 2025. While the implementation of management responses fell slightly to 86%, this was largely attributable to the introduction of a more rigorous monitoring and tracking system. The use of evaluation remains strong, with 90% of offices reporting the use of evaluation to inform strategic planning, strengthen program approaches, and identify new opportunities. This is also consistent with what we've seen at the corporate level, where the connection is being made between evaluations and planning. In the area of partnerships, the Independent Evaluation Service continued to co-convene the United Nations Evaluation Group Gender Equality, Disability, and Human Rights Working Group, and continued to serve as Secretariat for the UN SWAP Evaluation Performance Indicator. The Evaluation Service engaged in interagency humanitarian evaluations and UN system-wide evaluations and initiatives to ensure that evaluations incorporate gender equality. This includes leading an SDG 5 synthesis and co-chairing the People Pillar synthesis of the Global SDG Synthesis Coalition. In 2024, the Evaluation Service continued its partnerships for national evaluation capacity development and supported country-level evaluations of national gender strategies and policies, including the Liberia National Gender Policy Evaluation and a peacebuilding evaluation in Guatemala. Looking ahead, the Independent Evaluation Service will continue to conduct corporate strategic evaluations, provide technical assistance to decentralized evaluations, and build evaluation partnerships in the UN system. It will continue to place strong emphasis on strengthening evaluation use and communication. To conclude, despite constrained resources, there's sustained recognition from reviews like MOPAN or by the Joint Inspection Unit that evaluation in UN Women remains credible and critical to delivering results and strengthening impact. In this context, evaluation is not just a tool for accountability. Timely evaluation evidence remains essential for implementing and guiding UN Women's strategic plan strategies, informing programming at the country level. I extend my sincere appreciation to our team and for their dedication, and to management for their collaboration and commitment. And the Board can continue to rely on UN Women's robust, independent evaluation function to ensure that in times of uncertainty and constrained resources, the entity stays focused. And now, members of the Executive Board, I have the pleasure of presenting the results of the corporate evaluation of UN Women's support women's participation in peace processes. This work, conducted by the Independent Evaluation Service, supports accountability, learning, and strategic improvement. Since the adoption of the Beijing Platform for Action and Security Council Resolution 1325, evidence shows that women's participation in peace processes enhances the effectiveness of those peace processes. UN Women has been a strong advocate for ensuring that women and women's organizations are included at all levels of peace processes. Through these efforts, UN Women pushes for a more inclusive and effective approach to peace and security. The independent evaluation found that UN Women has made meaningful contributions in 5 core ways. First, by convening stakeholders, including women from across political, ethnic, and geographic divides, and this has helped to build common agendas and create opportunities for women to access decision-makers and peace actors. Second, by raising awareness and political commitment at national, regional, and global levels. UN Women has kept women's voices present in national peace frameworks and in regional bodies like the African Union and in UN Security Council deliberations, driving member-state accountability on women, peace, and security. Third, by supporting and accompanying civil society organizations, building their technical, organizational, and leadership capacity to influence peace processes from start to implementation. Fourth, by embedding gender equality and women, peace, and security in institutions and policy frameworks, such as national action plans and peace agreements, for example, in Colombia. And fifth, through partnerships, especially where UN Women has political access and local presence, for example, in Georgia, with the co-chairs of the Geneva International Discussion. Supporting women's participation in peace processes is deeply rooted in UN Women's unique integrated mandate and its consistent relationships with women's movements, especially those at the grassroots. UN Women brings voices to peace tables that are otherwise excluded. Sustainable results are found where UN Women supports the institutions, policies, and capacities to ensure that women's participation, even in the face of significant setbacks is there. Looking inside UN Women, the evaluation found that politically skilled personnel, senior representatives, presence in country, deep contextual knowledge, and enabling corporate procedures are critical drivers to deliver. The evaluation recommends that UN Women reinforce these areas. The evaluation also recommends focusing on women's capacity to engage in peace processes, building demand for women's participation, among peace process actors. Let me close with the powerful example of Colombia, where UN Women brought together more than 1,000 women from all different backgrounds, amplifying women's voices and strengthening women's influence to develop a unified agenda on peace. The evidence reinforces that investing in women's leadership is essential for lasting peace. UN Women's work in peace processes matters, and UN Women makes a difference. Thank you.

Excellencies, turning to the next evaluation I'm pleased to present management and corporate response to the corporate evaluation of UN Women's support to women's participation in peace processes. Let me start by recognizing your very strong statements yesterday and your strong commitment to the issue of women, peace and security, and echo the Executive Director's words that we need peace now more than ever. So as we respond to the evaluation, a report, I wanted to echo those words. The increasing volatile global context, the evolving nature of peace processes, and the deepening of backlash against the gender equality make the realization of the Women, Peace and Security Agenda more urgent and more complex. Allow me, Your Excellencies, to say some of us were born in war. I dream of peace every night. UN Women welcomes the evaluation's recognition of our contributions to advancing women's participation in peace processes. We are encouraged by the confirmation of our strong partnership with civil society, diverse women's groups and regional organizations, the sustainability of our work with national action plans and with member states, and our convening role in the fragile context. At the global level, our policy and coordination work with the UN Security Council, DPPA, the WPFs, and Humanitarian Action Compact and the Focal Points Network has ensured that women's voices and perspectives remain visible in international peace and security discussions. The evaluation offers timely and valuable recommendations, many of which are already informing our work. We recognize the need to strengthen political and diplomatic expertise in conflict contexts, We concur that increasing women's meaningful participation requires strengthening gender and conflict analysis, deepening political engagement, and enhancing partnership. These are very important issues in our evaluation also around resourcing. As UN Women agrees, agrees that stronger engagement with the peace process actors is necessary to drive consistent demand for women's participation to counter the gender backlash, and equally the importance of protection of women human rights defenders, including women peacebuilders, in strengthening coordination across the UN system to ensure protection, voice, and leadership, including through the Gender Equality Acceleration Plan. Your Excellencies, UN Women will act on the evaluation recommendations. However, we underscore that these actions are sustained flexible and predictable resources to be effectively implemented. Without adequate investment, our ability to deliver on these recommendations will be constrained. As we commemorate the 25th anniversary of Security Council Resolution 1325, we must treat this as a call to investment and recommit to inclusion and— to inclusive and sustainable peace with urgency that the current context demands. UN Women stands ready to work across country, region, and global levels to ensure that women lead, participate, and shape peace processes. When women lead, peace follows. Thank you, and I look forward to the discussion.

Thank you very much, Madam Vice President, for giving me the floor. I make this statement on behalf of Albania, Australia, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Latvia, Luxembourg, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Slovakia, Sweden, Türkiye, Uganda, the United Kingdom, and the European Union as a donor, and my own country, Switzerland. We especially want to highlight the commitment to the reform agenda by working in partnership for gender-responsive evaluations through UNEP, system-wide and joint evaluations, and engaging with MOPAN. We also highly welcome the progress in building internal evaluation capacity. Can IES share more details on the evaluation professionalization initiative? Only a few months remain till the end of 2025, and we thus encourage UN Women Management and IES to pay close attention to those 5 key performance indicators that do not appear close to reaching the 2025 targets. Let me respond to some of the specific questions that you have raised to my office. In terms of the professionalization initiative, this is indeed a unique function that we play to help all of UN Women improve its evaluation posture. And this is not new. It is a professionalization initiative that that we have been rolling out now for several years, and it's aimed at UN Women personnel, primarily those in managing evaluations, those in monitoring and evaluation functions. And it's focused around supporting them to acquire knowledge through our resource materials, through our handbooks, through e-learning courses, through coaching, but also applying that knowledge hands-on. In 2024, we reached many UN Women colleagues with learning sessions, with coaching, with hands-on support. For example, in Ecuador, in Liberia, and Central African Republic, we've seen progress in terms of the certification process of certain colleagues around evaluation. This is really important to ensure that there's a demand for evaluation and that there's a focus on evaluation to ensure that the prerequisites to be able to evaluate exist in programming. In terms of your questions on the targets and the evaluation implementation rate and how to reduce the number of small-scale evaluations, indeed, this is something we've been advocating for for some time. I think it comes from us advocating with management to prioritize strategic evaluations. Those are country portfolio evaluations, thematic evaluations, cluster evaluations. And it also relies on, I believe, also a trust of our donors, of our funding partners, to rely on those strategic evaluations to inform programming and to prioritize those. We can also do more in terms of ensuring, through our guidance to colleagues, that they advocate at field, country, and global level for reliance on strategic evaluations. And we can also help to ensure that funding is available for those strategic evaluations, particularly those at the country level. Country portfolio evaluations, strategic cluster evaluations, all require evaluation funding to be available and protected. On our strategy on evaluation use, indeed, an evaluation is as useful as it is used. We have been working to measure and to try to promote evaluation use since we have been in existence, yet it's a time to take a fresh look in terms of how can we further support evaluation use. And in this regard, we have conducted some outreach, conducted some surveys to understand what are some of the current bottlenecks around evaluation use to be able to inform programming and to inform decisions. And here what we want to do is really to build the culture and to build the demand for evaluations across UN Women. We want to make the evidence accessible and clear through strategic communications. And we want to ensure that the knowledge that is available is available— the knowledge that we create and report from evaluations is available across UN Women and across all stakeholders, civil society, others working in the sphere of gender equality. And in terms of the targets and funding, indeed, I agree, in times of crisis, oversight is essential for transparency. Transparency, integrity, and trust. It goes without saying that without funding, we are unable to conduct evaluations. We are unable to conduct some of our outreach. And I would highlight and just end here by saying that I believe we already have a very lean evaluation function. We conduct evaluations ourselves, and we do see and advocate for evaluations to take place at country level. However, we do see that resources are stretched, and that means that, for example, a country portfolio evaluation may take place only once over 2 strategic note cycles. So, essential to ensure that evaluation funding remains set, and we will continue to monitor that and report to you. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, members of the Executive Board, colleagues. Good morning again. I have the pleasure of presenting an overview of the Annual Report on Internal Audit and Investigation. With UN Women's mandate to deliver for all women and girls, it's crucial that all resources are used effectively and efficiently. Internal audit and investigation activities underpin trust and integrity. They help organizations to to reach their objectives in an accountable, fair, and transparent manner. In 2024, my office continued to be independent, with the freedom to decide on the scope of our work and to report on our work. We enjoyed full access to information and a seat at the table to provide evidence and advice to management in the stewardship of the organization. We are reliant upon the management to provide resources to deliver our mandate. At present, the Internal Audit Service can assess large and high-risk offices every 3 to 4 years, with medium-sized offices reached over a 7-year cycle. In 2024, UN Women established the Internal Investigation Function, demonstrating management's commitment to strengthening and supporting timely investigations into potential misconduct. While I recognize the challenging funding environment and reform, I highlight the need to ensure that resources are protected for oversight and that UN Women's internal investigation function is stably funded. Last year, we conducted work on 17 audit and advisory assignments. We issued 11 final reports, of which 9 were audits with overall opinions assessed. 5 entities or processes were assessed as satisfactory, the highest rating of a 4-tier system, and 4 were assessed as partially satisfactory, the second-highest ranking. This work formed the basis for our overall opinion that overall UN Women's governance risk management and controls were, in aggregate, satisfactory, with some improvements needed. We appreciate and highlight the continuing maturity of UN Women's governance and risk management. The transparency portal makes data widely accessible, and quarterly business reviews support organizational effectiveness objectives. In our annual opinion, we make 4 overarching objectives— observations, sorry. The second line, in terms of management oversight, is improving but needs further enhancement. More technical capacity should be available at decentralized levels. The statement of internal controls is progressing and should be finalized, and risks around cybersecurity and data governance should continue to be monitored and addressed. Looking globally, the pivot to regions and countries aims to shift UN Women's business model and culture. Given pressures on funding, management's indicated that the pivot should create cost savings is welcome. We also encourage UN Women to continue to focus on process efficiency and value for money to maximize impact and resources for results. We track actions that management takes to address our recommendations, and last year, following a rigorous review and follow-up effort, the percentage of long-outstanding internal audit recommendations decreased to 3%. This is a marked improvement from from previous years. Turning now to investigations. In 2024, UN Women launched a hybrid model for investigations, establishing an independent internal investigation function and continuing to engage the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services as an external investigations provider. UN OIOS continues to handle intake of all UN Women complaints, and in 2024, there were 76 new allegations of potential misconduct, up from 63 reported in the previous year. The increase in types of allocations are consistent, in my view, with trends across international organizations and reflects positively on the growing awareness of reporting mechanisms as well as management control measures that are designed to identify risks and red flags in a timely manner. 71 cases were closed in 2024, of which 62 were closed after preliminary assessment, and 9 were closed after investigation. Of the 62 cases closed after preliminary assessment, OIOS referred 39 cases to my office for consideration on potential action. Looking ahead, and before closing, Madam Chair, I'd like to highlight some goals and priorities as we seek to support UN Women in a rapidly changing and challenging environment. We will continue to provide timely assurance on key risks. risks that emerge as a trusted advisor. Madam Chair, distinguished delegates and colleagues, thank you for the opportunity to introduce the report on the activities of the UN Women Ethics Function for 2024 in accordance with Executive Board Decision 2022/5. The mandate of the Ethics Function is to cultivate and nurture a culture of ethics, integrity, and accountability, and thereby enhance the trust in and credibility of the United Nations, both internally and externally. From 2023 to 2024, the foundations were put in place to ensure that conflicts of interest could be more effectively mitigated and managed by the organization, and to strengthen UN Women's procedures and policies on protection against retaliation. The Outside Activities Policy and Procedure, as well as the revised Protection Against Retaliation Policy, were issued in early 2024 and represent important steps in embedding ethics in UN Women's policies. I was also routinely invited to comment on revisions to other policies, ensuring that an ethics perspective is reflected. These policy foundations need to be complemented with a significant investment in outreach and awareness-raising to support an ethical culture. In 2024, the Ethics Function engaged in robust outreach efforts to further strengthen awareness with respect to the core values of independence, integrity, and impartiality that apply to all UN Women personnel, with 670 UN Women participations during the reporting period. In addition to delivering tailored training sessions on ethical standards, conflicts of interest, and protection against retaliation at HQ, regional, and country offices, the ethics function sought to expand its outreach efforts to support engagement with UN Women personnel on the importance of upholding ethical standards with its first-ever Joint Ethics Awareness Month and the Leadership Dialogue. In order to amplify impact on a critical and timely topic, UN Women Ethics partnered with the UNDP Ethics Office to launch an Ethics Awareness Month on the topic, Navigating Impartiality in a Polarized World. The topic was particularly relevant given the number of elections in 2024 and UN Women's close working relationships with governments to support gender equality. The topic for the 2024 Leadership Dialogue was Navigating Outside Activities. 1,746 UN Women personnel participated, the highest participation level ever for a dialogue at UN Women. The advisory role is essential in fostering an ethical organizational culture and supporting proactive risk management. During the reporting period, 64% of requests for ethics services were requests for advice. This is a 121% increase from the 160 advisory requests received during the 9-month period from April 1st to December 31st, 2023. The increase is contributable attributable to the comparison period, 9 months in 2023 and a full year in '24, the issuance of the Outside Activities Policy, the growing level of visibility of the ethics function due to outreach efforts and the support of senior management, as well as increased trust that the ethics function will provide timely, independent, confidential, and actionable advice. Conflict of interest risk is also identified, mitigated, and managed through UN Women's investigation and the UN Financial Disclosure Program. In 2024, 100% of UN Women filers submitted their disclosure statements as required. During the reporting period, I received 5 inquiries under the Protection Against Retaliation policy. 4 were requests for advice. In the one request for protection, the complainant requested the suspension of the review. In a matter referred for investigation to OIOS by the UN Ethics Office in 2022, I made a final determination in '24 that retaliation had not occurred. I continued to be an active member of IPON and ENMO during 2024 and attended the annual ENMO conference hosted by WHO in Geneva, which was followed by a mission to UN Women personnel. From January 1st, 2025, I was appointed as the alternate chair of IPON, which you will hear more about in next year's report. In 2025, the ethics function is focusing on continuing to positively influence organizational culture through training on ethics, ethical standards, timely addressing the growing demands to proactively mitigate and manage conflict of interest risk, and engaging with personnel at the onboarding stage to increase awareness of the ethical behavior expected of all UN Women personnel. The independence of the ethics function is fundamental to the effective delivery of its mandates. The function conducts its activities free from external interference and reports directly to the executive director. However, as is noted in the report, the ethics function continues to operate without sufficient long-term resources to enable the sustainable implementation of its mandates. Adequate resources need to be devoted to ensure timely service delivery, targeted outreach efforts to support an ethical organizational culture, and to meet the growing demand for advice on risk due to organizational changes. I wish to thank my colleague Mercedes for outstanding work since her arrival last October. I wish to thank the Executive Board for its continued support of the ethics function and will be pleased to answer any questions that you may have. Thank you, Madam Chair.

We note the steps taken to strengthen accountability, especially the review and update of the Protection Against Retaliation Policy. These safeguards matter. They are more than paperwork. They are promises made real. We welcome the surge in learning and outreach. The record participation in the 2024 Leadership Dialogue on Outside Activities speaks volumes. Ethics is not an add-on. It is an integral part to the leadership of every day and every level. We also applaud the collaboration with UNDP to launch the first Joint Ethics Awareness Month. This is the future— coherence across the system, unity in principle. UN Women remains fully compliant with the Financial Disclosure Programme. This is essential not just to detect and manage conflicts of interest, but to preserve the confidence of those we serve. Ethics is not just about rules. It's about people, about creating an environment where colleagues can raise concerns freely, where they can speak openly and act boldly without fear of retaliation. We thank the Ethics Function for its continued guidance on these sensitive matters, and for timely referrals in line with protocol. Excellencies, system-wide coherence matters too. That's why we fully support continued participation in UN forums, such as the Ethics Panel and the Multilateral Ethics Network. Shared learning strengthens us all. UN Women remains firmly committed to ensuring that the ethics function is fully independent and adequately resourced. An ethical culture does not arise by chance. It is built, safeguarded, and respected. Looking ahead, we must define what a properly resourced ethics function should look like. We cannot continue to do more with less. For every internal support or oversight function, or second line of defense we fund, we must weigh the impact on the resources available for the women and girls we serve. Given our current financial constraints and guided by the UNAID principles of streamlining and coherence, we are actively exploring ways to establish a shared service model for the ethics function with other agencies, We will continue to examine these options, and we will report back to you on progress. Finally, I wish to sincerely thank our Ethics Officer Advisor, Sarah Labour, for her outstanding service. She has helped shape a function that is rigorous, resilient, and trusted. We wish her continued success as she takes on her next chapter. As she moves on, UN Women remains committed on building on the strong foundation she leaves behind, ensuring ethics continues to anchor our work and inspire our way forward. With that, I thank you.
